newsitem.title: USA: Fla. Windstorm Association to sell $500 mln notes.
newsitem.headline: Fla. Windstorm Association to sell $500 mln notes.

text.p: The Florida Windstorm Underwriting Association will sell $500 million of taxable, 10-year notes on Thursday in a private placement, officials involved in the deal said Monday.
Chase Manhattan Investment Services Inc will be the lead underwriter for the deal, which will be the first debt sale by the Windstorm Association.
Officials at the assocition declined to comment, citing the mandatory quiet period for privately placed issues.

Barbara Byche, a director at Standard & Poor's Corp, said the sale is similar to the $500 million taxable note sale completed in May by another state insurance pool, the Florida Residential Property and Casualty Joint Underwriting Association.

"It's very similar to the JUA deal," Byche said. "Both of these, the JUA and the Windstorm Association issued what they considered 'pre-event' notes to have funding on hand just in case a storm hit, so they would have some cash flow to pay out," Bych said.
"The thought is that if they were to issue at the time of the event the rates wouldn't be as marketable," she said.
She said the Windstorm Association sought private placement because the deal is fairly sophisticated.
The Florida Windstorm Association was created by the state legislature in 1970 to insure policyholders in the Florida Keys against damage from from hurricanes, windstorms, tornadoes, and hail.

Other coastal counties have been added to the coverage area and the association now holds about 500,000 policies. Its potential exposure to a catastrophic 500-year hurricane could result in losses of up to $8.298 billion, S&P said in its rating report.

The association has the authority to levy special assessments on insurance companies that do business in Florida to cover any deficits from a surge in claims, but it is barred from building up any surplus in advance.
Unlike the JUA deal, the Windstorm Association deal has a mandatory defeasement schedule, Byche said.

Florida has three major insurance pool programs. In addition to the Windstorm Association, the JUA was formed after Hurricane Andrew and is the insurer of last resort for homeowners unable to find insurance on the commercial market.

The third pool, the Hurricane Catastrophe Fund, acts as a reinsurer for insurance companies and is also planning an intitial debt issue, a $500 revenue bond sale. The fund is awaiting bond validation in the Florida Supreme Court and fund officials said the sale would not take place at least until after the hurricane season ends on Nov. 30.
